mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding sensitivity last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild sensitivity after composite bonding is common and is generally considered a normal part of the settling-in process. For most patients, any heightened sensitivity — particularly to cold temperatures or air — begins to ease within the first three to five days and typically resolves fully within one to two weeks. If sensitivity is significant, worsening, or continues beyond two weeks, it is advisable to contact your dental practice so the bonded tooth can be properly assessed. A qualified dentist can determine whether the sensitivity relates to the bonding itself or to an underlying tooth concern that may need attention.

mainEntity.name: Can composite bonding change how I speak?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, particularly when bonding is applied to the front teeth, patients notice a very slight change in how certain sounds are produced — for example, a minor lisp or unfamiliar feeling when forming words with "s" or "th" sounds. This is because the tongue is adjusting to the altered tooth shape. For the vast majority of patients, any speech adjustment is subtle and resolves naturally within a few days as the tongue adapts. If speech feels notably affected beyond the first week, it is worth mentioning to your dentist at your follow-up.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for composite bonding to feel rough?

acceptedAnswer.text: Immediately after composite bonding is placed and polished, the surface should feel smooth. However, some patients notice subtle texture differences compared to natural enamel, particularly as the tongue explores unfamiliar contours. A very minor surface roughness at the edges can sometimes be refined during a quick follow-up appointment. If you notice rough edges, sharp points, or anything that is irritating your tongue or cheek tissue, contact your dental practice — this is a simple matter for your dentist to address and should not be left untreated as it may cause irritation to the soft tissues over time.

Composite bonding is securely adhered to the tooth surface through a process involving etching and bonding agents. However, like all restorations, it is not indestructible. Bonding can chip or detach if subjected to significant force — such as biting very hard foods, accidental impact, or habits like nail biting. If a piece of composite bonding comes away, keep the fragment if possible and contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment. Avoid attempting any self-repair. Your dentist will evaluate the tooth and advise on the best approach to restore the bonding appropriately.

Composite resin is matched carefully to the shade and translucency of your surrounding teeth, and when applied by an experienced dentist, the results can appear very natural. However, composite resin does not reflect light in exactly the same way as natural enamel or porcelain, and colour matching can be influenced by lighting conditions, hydration of the tooth at the time of placement, and individual enamel characteristics. Maintaining good oral hygiene and attending regular check-ups will help preserve the appearance of composite bonding over time. Your dentist will discuss realistic expectations with you during your consultation.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my composite bonding needs adjusting?

acceptedAnswer.text: The clearest signs that composite bonding may need adjustment include: a bite that feels consistently uneven when chewing or closing the jaw; persistent discomfort in the bonded tooth or surrounding jaw; visible chipping or fracture of the resin material; or a noticeable change in the appearance of the bonding, such as discolouration or lifting at the edges. Minor bite refinements are straightforward and routine. Any of these concerns are worth raising with your dental team sooner rather than later, as early assessment generally leads to simpler and more effective management.
